name: Microcurietherapy

lead: Microcurietherapy is a historical theory, proposed in the early 1910s by French pharmacist Alexandre Jaboin, that very small doses of radium would stimulate living cells and increase their energy. It was inspired by the success of radium (curie) therapy against some cancers.

In the decades that followed, radium and thorium appeared in cosmetics and tonics promising rejuvenation and a youthful look, such as the French Tho-Radia line sold from 1932. Wikipedia says the theory was never scientifically demonstrated.

paras: Historically the idea was applied through creams, powders, soaps, toothpaste and tonics containing small amounts of radium or thorium compounds. Tho-Radia's cream, for instance, was advertised with an image of a glowing young woman. Nothing here describes current practice.

Radioactive consumer products are associated with documented harm; the Radithor drinker Eben Byers died in 1932 after heavy use. Regulations in France from 1937 led Tho-Radia to drop radium. Regulators today warn that some products sold with 'negative ion' claims may contain uranium or thorium.

chain: Tiny radium dose applied to skin
angle.text: Historical products used radioactive ingredients on the promise of rejuvenated skin. The appearance benefit was claimed in advertising and was not shown in studies.

lead: Microcurietherapy is the name given to a theory attributed to French pharmacist Alexandre Jaboin in the early 1910s: that very small doses of radium would stimulate living cells and increase their energy.[1] It took inspiration from the success of brachytherapy, or curietherapy, in treating certain cancers.[1]

Wikipedia says the theory was never scientifically demonstrated but helped start a trend of radium-based medicines and cosmetics in the 1910s, including products that sold the idea of renewed, youthful skin.[1][2]

The best-known cosmetic embodiment was Tho-Radia, a French line sold from 1932 to 1968, which began with a cream and expanded to toothpaste, soap, powder, perfume and lipstick, with advertising showing a young woman lit by rays.[1] Radium and thorium were included at first; after new rules in 1937 the brand dropped radium.[1]
infobox: French rules from 1937 ended radium in Tho-Radia[1]

paras: After the discovery of radioactive decay in 1896, radium was promoted as a cure-all, and the early 20th century saw many radioactive consumer goods.[2] Jaboin's idea of stimulating cells with small doses supported the trend.[1]

Tho-Radia was developed by pharmacist Alexis Moussalli with Dr Alfred Curie, who was unrelated to Pierre and Marie Curie; the brand was registered in November 1932 and used the line 'after Dr Alfred Curie's formula'.[1] A 1932 lab analysis found a trace of radium in the cream.[1] Sales declined after Moussalli's death in 1955, the company was sold to Lafarge in 1962 and the brand was abandoned in 1968.[1]

Wikipedia's page on radioactive quackery lists Radithor, a radium salt solution claimed to be curative, which industrialist Eben Byers drank in large quantities from 1927 to 1930 before dying in 1932; Doramad toothpaste with thorium; and Revigator pots adding radon to drinking water.[2] Other cosmetic brands named in the Radium Girls article include Artes, Ramey, Radior and Tho-Radia.[3]
No studies found. Wikipedia states the stimulation theory was never scientifically demonstrated.[1]

The US Nuclear Regulatory Commission and state agencies have warned that some modern 'negative ion' products may contain uranium or thorium, and anti-5G necklaces found radioactive have drawn warnings.[2]

timeline.event: Radioactive decay discovered; radium soon promoted for health.[2]
Tho-Radia brand registered and launched in Paris; Eben Byers dies after Radithor use.[1][2]
